summary: Sirach 39 first describes the learned scribe: he studies the law, ancient wisdom, prophecies, proverbs, and parables, prays for pardon, and teaches what he has received. The chapter then turns into a hymn calling readers to praise the Lord for all his works, including both the goods that sustain life and the forces of judgment that the text says serve God’s command. It closes by insisting that God supplies every need in its proper time and calling for praise with heart and voice.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins two major concerns of Sirach: disciplined study and praise of God as creator and ruler. It also shows how the book connects wisdom, prayer, public teaching, and the difficult claim that all created things have their appointed use.

context.author: Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora who wanted to live according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, Torah study, scribal learning, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture all in view.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction that uses poetic teaching, direct address, hymn, catalogue, and praise.

outline.heading: The Work of the Scribe
outline.note: The chapter begins by contrasting the wise student with others: he gives himself to the law of the Most High, studies ancient wisdom, prophecies, sayings, proverbs, and parables, and serves in public settings.

outline.heading: Prayer and Gifted Understanding
outline.note: The scribe rises to seek the Lord, prays for pardon, receives understanding if the Lord wills, and teaches what he has learned.

outline.heading: A Lasting Reputation
outline.note: His understanding is praised, his memory endures, nations declare his wisdom, and his name outlasts his life.

outline.heading: Call to Praise
outline.note: The speaker, filled with what he has considered, urges the holy children to flourish, give fragrance, sing praise, and bless the Lord for all his works.

outline.heading: God’s Works and Timing
outline.note: The hymn says the Lord’s works are good, his commands come in their time, nothing is hidden from him, and his ways are plain to the holy but stumbling blocks to the wicked.

outline.heading: Created Goods and Instruments of Judgment
outline.note: The chapter lists necessary goods for human life, then names destructive forces and creatures as things prepared for vengeance and subject to God’s command.

outline.heading: Written Conviction and Final Praise
outline.note: The speaker summarizes his conviction in writing: all the Lord’s works are good, each is approved in its time, and the proper response is praise.

keyVerses.text: Not so he who has applied his soul and meditates in the law of the Most High. He will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients and will be occupied with prophecies.
keyVerses.why: This verse opens the portrait of the learned scribe and shows that his wisdom is rooted in sustained study of law, ancient teaching, and prophecy.

keyVerses.text: If the great Lord wills, he will be filled with the spirit of understanding; he will pour forth the words of his wisdom and in prayer give thanks to the Lord.
keyVerses.why: The scribe’s learning is not presented as self-made expertise alone; the chapter ties understanding to God’s will and to prayer.

keyVerses.text: All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good, and every command will be done in its time.
keyVerses.why: This begins the hymn’s central claim: God’s works are good and ordered by appointed timing.

keyVerses.text: All the works of the Lord are good. He will supply every need in its time.
keyVerses.why: Near the end, the chapter repeats and condenses its conviction about creation, divine provision, and timing.

themes: study of law and ancient wisdom
created things and their appointed uses
good, evil, and judgment in due time

questions.question: Who is the main figure in the first part of the chapter?
questions.answer: The first eleven verses describe a learned scribe or wisdom teacher. He studies the law of the Most High, ancient wisdom, prophecies, sayings, proverbs, and parables, and he also serves among rulers and travels among nations. The chapter presents study, prayer, public service, and teaching as parts of one vocation.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by “law of the Most High”?
questions.answer: The phrase names the sacred instruction in which the wise person meditates. Sirach forms students to live within Israel’s covenant, so this is Torah-shaped learning joined to practice. Verse 1 links that sustained study with ancient wisdom and prophecy.

questions.question: Why does the wise person pray for pardon if he is being praised?
questions.answer: The portrait does not treat learning as moral perfection. Verse 5 says he seeks the Lord, prays, and asks pardon for his sins before verse 6 speaks of being filled with understanding if the Lord wills. The chapter holds scholarship, humility, and dependence on God together.

questions.question: Does Sirach promise that every wise teacher will become famous?
questions.answer: Verses 9–11 complete an ideal portrait of the learned teacher: many commend him, nations declare his wisdom, and his name lives on. The elevated praise presents wisdom as a public good with a lasting legacy. It does not set out conditions or a timetable by which every wise teacher becomes famous.

questions.question: Why does the chapter suddenly move from the scribe to praise of creation?
questions.answer: Verse 12 marks a transition: the speaker says he has more to utter and is filled like the full moon. From there, he calls the “holy children” to praise and then sings about the Lord’s works. The movement suggests that true wisdom does not end with study; it becomes public praise and reflection on the world under God’s command.

questions.question: What is the point of asking, “What is this?” and “Why is that?”
questions.answer: The repeated question challenges the reader’s impulse to dismiss parts of creation as useless or badly timed. Verses 17 and 21 answer that things are sought out or understood at the proper time and that all things are created for their own uses. The chapter is making a wisdom claim about limits on human judgment.

questions.question: What does “heathen” mean here?
questions.answer: In verse 23, “heathen” refers to peoples portrayed as outside the holy or godly group assumed by the speaker. The verse links them with wrath, while verse 24 contrasts the holy and the wicked. The chapter’s language is ancient boundary-making language, and it should be described as such rather than turned directly into a modern label for whole peoples.

questions.question: How can the chapter say both good things and evil things are created?
questions.answer: The chapter says necessities such as water and food serve the godly but become harmful to sinners. It then names fire, hail, famine, death, beasts, and weapons as instruments of judgment that obey God’s command. This is a strong claim about divine rule over destructive forces, but the poem does not explain every disaster or identify the guilt of each person who suffers one.

questions.question: What final response does the chapter ask from readers?
questions.answer: The chapter ends by repeating the claim that the Lord’s works are good and timely. It then turns from explanation to response: “with all your hearts and voices,” readers are called to sing praises and bless the Lord’s name. The closing focus is not mastery of every mystery, but praise after reflection.

glossary.def: A title for God in this chapter, used where the wise person meditates in God’s law and makes supplication before God.
Compact teaching sayings or comparisons whose subtleties and dark sayings the wise person seeks to understand.
A fragrant substance used here as an image for the pleasing praise the speaker urges from the holy children.
A poetic name for wine, included here among the necessities for human life.
A word for heavy blows or punishments, used when the chapter describes winds created for vengeance.
